content: 1. The Xpert diagnostic technology offers rapid results, typically within hours rather than weeks. It is automated, does not require fresh samples for optimal performance, and does not necessitate stringent laboratory containment measures. 2. Direct testing of sputum without centrifugation reduces the risk of cross-contamination. 3. In 2017, the Foundation for Innovative New Diagnostics (FIND) conducted evaluations comparing Xpert assays to the reference standard of culture using sputum samples collected in clinical settings across various countries. 4. The sensitivity and specificity of the Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra assays, as measured in the FIND evaluations, were used to inform WHO policy recommendations for clinical management. Sensitivity for Xpert MTB/RIF was 83% (range: 78–87%), and specificity was 98% (range: 96–99%). For Xpert Ultra, assuming trace results as positive, sensitivity was 88% (range: 84–91%) and specificity was 95% (range: 93–97%). 5. The FIND study collected up to four sputum samples per individual and conducted multiple tests, including 2–3 Ultra tests, 1 Xpert MTB/RIF test, 2–3 solid cultures (LJ), 2–3 liquid cultures (MGIT), and 2 smears. Sensitivity and specificity estimates were based on the first Xpert test and classified patients as MTB-positive if any culture was positive for M. tuberculosis. 6. The 2017 FIND evaluation results align with a 2021 Cochrane systematic review, which also highlighted limitations in other studies and reviews. 7. Lower sensitivity of Xpert assays means that prevalence surveys relying on Xpert as the primary diagnostic or screening test may miss cases that could have been detected using liquid culture. 8. The specificity of Xpert MTB/RIF (96–99%) and Xpert Ultra (93–97%) reflects the ability of these assays to detect DNA regardless of bacilli viability. This can result in positive Xpert results even when TB bacilli are dead, leading to false-positive results. 9. A study in Vietnam tested all adults in a community with Xpert MTB/RIF, regardless of TB symptoms. Among those with positive Xpert results, 61% had positive culture results. The study estimated sensitivity and specificity of Xpert MTB/RIF in the general population at 69% and 99%, respectively. 10. The specificity of Xpert assays in national TB prevalence surveys was consistent with FIND evaluations and a 2021 systematic review. However, sensitivity was lower in prevalence surveys compared to clinical settings. 11. Xpert Ultra incorporates two new multicopy amplification targets (IS6110 and IS1081) and a larger DNA amplification reaction chamber compared to Xpert MTB/RIF. Its semi-quantitative scale includes trace, very low, low, medium, and high. Trace results indicate the lowest bacillary burden and detection of multicopy targets only. 12. In national TB prevalence surveys, the proportion of screen-positive individuals with culture-positive TB disease is typically low (1–5%). This means that most individuals tested in a survey will be culture-negative, and a small percentage will have false-positive Xpert results. 13. Recent prevalence surveys in Lesotho and South Africa used both Xpert Ultra and liquid culture. Sensitivity of Ultra was 80% in Lesotho and 78% in South Africa, assuming trace results were TB-positive. 14. The pooled sensitivity of Xpert MTB/RIF in prevalence surveys was 73% (range: 62–82%), and specificity was 99% (range: 98–99%). For Xpert Ultra, pooled sensitivity was 78% (range: 69–84%), and specificity was 98% (range: 96–99%). 15. Sensitivity and specificity of Xpert Ultra were lower for individuals with a past history of TB disease compared to those without such a history. This is likely due to the detection of dead TB bacilli or DNA fragments in individuals with prior TB. 16. In prevalence surveys, Xpert Ultra may detect TB cases missed by solid culture testing, particularly in individuals at earlier stages of the disease. 17. The sensitivity of Xpert assays in prevalence surveys is likely lower than in clinical settings because surveys often identify smear-negative pulmonary cases, which are harder to detect. 18. Sensitivity can be improved by repeating Xpert testing on another sample and interpreting the combination as positive if at least one test is positive. 19. The specificity of Xpert assays in prevalence surveys may be slightly better than in clinical settings if the prevalence of individuals with a prior history of TB disease is lower in the community. 20. The pooled sensitivity estimates for Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra in prevalence surveys were based on a small number of surveys with wide credibility intervals, and no significant statistical difference in sensitivity between the two tests was demonstrated.
